papers.title_in_file: QUANTUM IN PRODUCTION: OPTIMIZING E-COMMERCE LOGISTICS (CASE STORY)
papers.what_it_is: A D-Wave marketing case story describing how the Pattison Food Group used D-Wave technology to automate weekly delivery driver scheduling, with reported time savings and deployment date.

assertions.value: The paper reports that the auto-scheduler cut a weekly task from 80 hours to 15 hours, which it states as an 80% time savings, and that it was deployed into production in late 2022.
assertions.anchor: Page 1, paragraph beginning 'The auto-scheduler is saving'; repeated on page 2
quotes: trimming what was once an 80-hour task to just 15 hours each week, an 80% time savings.
It was deployed into production in late 2022.
assertions.certainty_reason: A vendor case story reports a customer's figures with no method, baseline definition or measurement shown.
assertions.reader_inference: The savings from 80 to 15 hours is 65 hours, which is about 81 percent, so the stated 80 percent is a rounded figure. The paper gives no measurement method or comparison against a classical scheduler.

assertions.value: The paper states that driver schedules were built manually by a team of three to four e-commerce driver schedulers, and that this accounts for 80 person-hours of work each week.
quotes: Until recently, managing the driver schedules for those orders was a manual task.
a team of three to four e-commerce driver schedulers that creates schedules for all drivers, all across the provinces,
This accounts for 80 person-hours of work to build out the schedule for each week.
assertions.certainty_reason: A statement by a company manager relayed in a vendor case story; no records are shown.
assertions.reader_inference: The only baseline is the previous manual process. The paper does not compare the quantum approach with a classical optimization solver.

assertions.value: The paper describes PFG as the largest purveyor of food and healthcare products in western Canada, with more than 100 retail locations offering online ordering.
quotes: PFG is the largest purveyor of food and healthcare products in western Canada, with more than 100 retail locations offering online ordering.
assertions.certainty_reason: A description of the customer in a vendor document.

assertions.value: The paper reports that success was measured against a threshold of 95% of e-commerce shopper demand and against drivers receiving schedules that meet their expectations, and that Wai says each of the 100+ stores offering online ordering consistently meets these objectives.
quotes: Success was measured by a number of metrics, which included the ability to meet a threshold of 95% of the demand from the company’s e-commerce shoppers
each of the 100+ stores offering online ordering are consistently meeting these objectives.
assertions.certainty_reason: An interviewee's statement in a vendor case story; the paper shows no measured data per store.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper does not say how the demand coverage or driver expectations were measured, or what the values were before the auto-scheduler.

assertions.value: The paper lists scheduling factors the system must handle, including which stores a driver is willing and able to get to, how many drivers each shift needs, and a minimum of 10 hours between shifts, and states that the number of variables and constraints adds to the complexity.
assertions.anchor: Page 1, paragraphs 5 and 6 (the list continues across the page break)
quotes: which stores a given driver is willing and able to get to, how many drivers are needed on each shift,
ensure that time between each shift is at least 10 hours, and other considerations.
The number of variables and constraints contribute to the complexity of developing optimal schedules.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own description of the problem it set out to solve.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper gives no formulation, variable count or constraint count, so problem size cannot be judged from it.

assertions.value: The paper states the goal of the auto-scheduler as assigning each driver a weekly work assignment under user-designated constraints, so that each team member can work as many or as few shifts as they wish in a convenient and familiar location.
quotes: The auto-scheduler made it possible to assign drivers a weekly work assignment taking into account all manner of user-designated constraints,
each team member could work as many or as few shifts as they wish while operating in a convenient and familiar location.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own statement of what the application is meant to do.

assertions.value: The paper states that after the problems were mathematically formulated, the PFG team built a computational pipeline that enabled the D-Wave platform to formulate an effective autoscheduling solution.
quotes: Once these problems were mathematically formulated, the PFG team built out a computational pipeline that enabled the D-Wave platform to formulate an effective autoscheduling solution.
assertions.certainty_reason: A vendor's description of how its platform was used, with no technical detail.
assertions.reader_inference: The text names no solver type (for example annealing or hybrid), no problem formulation, no qubit or variable counts, no run times and no solution quality measures. The quantum contribution to the savings cannot be separated from the effect of automating a manual task.

assertions.value: The paper states that in the early days of the pandemic PFG began exploring quantum computing to automate shift-scheduling at individual stores, and that success with this initial test inspired the company to automate shift assignments for every driver in their fleet.
quotes: In the early days of the pandemic, the company began exploring the use of quantum computing to automate shift-scheduling tasks at individual stores.

assertions.certainty_reason: A vendor's account of the customer's project history; no results of the initial test are shown.

papers.what_it_is: An experimental paper reporting an all-passive anti-PT-symmetric three-waveguide structure on thin-film lithium niobate, with thermal tuning, equal power splitting, synchronized amplitude modulation and a transition to the broken phase.

assertions.value: The authors report an all-passive realization of anti-parity-time (anti-PT) optics on a thin-film lithium niobate on insulator (LNOI) nanophotonic platform, built from three waveguides with engineered lateral coupling and loss.
quotes: In this work, we report an all-passive realization of antiPT optics on a versatile nanophotonic platform of thin-
lithium niobate on insulator (LNOI)
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own platform and scope in the introduction.

assertions.value: The authors state that, before this work, anti-PT symmetry had only been realized in bulky systems or with optical gain.
quotes: Despite exciting progress, so far anti-PT symmetry has only been realized in bulky systems or with optical gain.

assertions.value: The authors state that anti-PT effects had been observed in cold atoms, electrical circuits and, very recently, integrated photonics with balanced loss and gain induced by Brillouin scattering.

papers.what_it_is: An experimental noise analysis of telecom to 775 nm sum frequency conversion with a small detuned telecom pump in an 8 mm periodically poled thin-film lithium niobate nanowaveguide, attributing noise to Raman scattering and SPDC after residual second harmonic generation.

assertions.value: The authors state that the device is an 8 mm long PPLN nanowaveguide on a 500 nm thick, X cut, magnesium doped lithium niobate thin film bonded on silicon dioxide on a silicon base, with a top width of 1.8 µm, a poling period of 2.5 µm, and a chip temperature stabilized at 48±0.1 degree.
quotes: an 8-mm long PPLN nanowaveguide is fabricated on a 500 nm thick, X-cut, magnesiumdoped lithium niobate thin film bonded on silicon dioxide
The top width is measured to be 1.8 µm.

The chip is placed on a stage whose temperature is stabilized at 48±0.1 degree.

papers.what_it_is: A pure-mathematics paper that defines a quantum automorphism group of a finite directed hypergraph, shows it generalizes Bichon's group for graphs, and shows it acts on hypergraph C*-algebras.

assertions.certainty_reason: Theorem 4.3 with proof.

assertions.value: The paper proves that for a simple graph encoded as an undirected hypergraph, Aut+(Γ) equals Bichon's quantum automorphism group.
quotes: Theorem 4.7. Let Γ be a simple graph. Then Aut+(Γ) = AutB+ic(Γ).
assertions.certainty_reason: Theorem 4.7 with proof.

assertions.value: The paper proves that for a multigraph without isolated vertices, encoded as a hypergraph, Aut+(Γ) equals the Goswami-Hossain quantum automorphism group in Bichon's sense.
quotes: Theorem 4.11. Let Γ be a multigraph without isolated vertices. Then
assertions.certainty_reason: Theorem 4.11 with proof.

assertions.value: The paper proves that, writing Ns(v) for the number of edges whose source set contains v, Ns(v) uvw = uvw Ns(w) for all vertices v, w. In particular uvw = 0 whenever Ns(v) differs from Ns(w). The same holds for the range map.
quotes: Ns(v) · uvw = uvw · Ns(w) ∀v, w ∈ V.
In particular, Ns(v) = Ns(w) implies uvw = 0.
assertions.certainty_reason: Proposition 4.6 with proof.
assertions.reader_inference: The text layer prints the in-particular condition as Ns(v) = Ns(w); by the proof it means the two counts are different.

assertions.value: The paper defines the hypergraph C*-algebra as the universal C*-algebra generated by mutually orthogonal projections p_v and partial isometries s_e with three relations. It states that a directed graph encoded as a hypergraph gives the classical graph C*-algebra.
quotes: If a directed graph is encoded as a hypergraph as in Deﬁnition 2.11, then the corresponding hypergraph C∗-algebra agrees with the classical graph C∗-algebra.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own definition and the reduction to graph algebras.

assertions.value: The paper constructs a unital *-homomorphism alpha from C*(Γ) to C*(Γ) tensor C(Aut+(Γ)) with alpha(p_v) the sum over w of p_w tensor u_wv and alpha(s_e) the sum over f of s_f tensor u_fe.
quotes: Then there exists a unital ∗-homomorphism
α(se) = sf ⊗ ufe ∀e ∈ E.
assertions.certainty_reason: Lemma 5.2 with proof.

assertions.value: The paper proves that Aut+(Γ) acts faithfully on the hypergraph C*-algebra C*(Γ) via the map alpha of Lemma 5.2.
quotes: Theorem 5.3. Let Γ be a hypergraph. Then Aut+(Γ) acts faithfully on C∗(Γ) via the map α from Lemma 5.2.
assertions.certainty_reason: Theorem 5.3 with proof.

assertions.value: The authors state that their quantum automorphism group is no longer maximal with respect to the Schmidt-Weber action on the graph C*-algebra, although the action equals the Schmidt-Weber one for classical graphs.
quotes: but our quantum automorphism group is no longer maximal with respect to it.
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated in the introduction; the paper gives no separate proof.

assertions.value: The authors state that for a classical directed graph, the action alpha reduces to the Schmidt-Weber action of Aut+Bic(Γ) on the graph C*-algebra, and note it was already shown by Joardar and Mandal that Aut+Bic(Γ) acts this way.
quotes: Hence, we obtain the action of Schmidt-Weber for AutB+ic(Γ) as a special case.
assertions.certainty_reason: Reduction stated in a remark.

assertions.value: The paper proves that Aut+(Γ) is the largest compact matrix quantum group acting faithfully on both C*(Γ) and C*(Γ') (Γ' the dual with source and range swapped) with the stated action formulas: any such G is a subgroup of Aut+(Γ).
quotes: Then G ⊆ Aut+(Γ).
Then Aut+(Γ) is the largest compact matrix quantum group which acts faithfully on both C∗(Γ) and C∗(Γ′)

assertions.certainty_reason: Lemma 5.7 with proof.

assertions.value: The paper defines a magic unitary over a finite set as a matrix of projections whose rows and columns each sum to the unit, and states that magic unitaries with entries in the complex numbers are exactly the classical permutation matrices.
quotes: Magic unitaries are also called quantum permutations since magic unitaries with entries in C are exactly classical permutation matrices.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own definition.

assertions.value: The paper cites Wang for the result that the quantum permutation group S_X+ is the largest compact matrix quantum group acting on C^X, so S_X+ is the quantum automorphism group of a finite set.
quotes: Thus, we can think of SX+ as the quantum automorphism group of a ﬁnite set X.
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the paper attributes to Wang [31].

assertions.value: The authors state that magic unitaries have applications in quantum information via non-local games, citing Lupini, Mancinska and Roberson.
quotes: These matrices have applications in quantum information via non-local games [19]
assertions.certainty_reason: A cited application, not developed in this paper.

assertions.value: The authors state that the class of hypergraph C*-algebras includes all graph C*-algebras and also new examples of non-nuclear C*-algebras.
quotes: This new class includes all graph C∗-algebras but also new examples of non-nuclear C∗-

assertions.value: The paper states as open the quantum automorphism group of the complete hypergraph on V. Since it has no multi-edges, Aut+ is a subgroup of SV+, but it is open whether the inclusion is proper.
quotes: However, it remains open if this inclusion is proper or if Aut+(Γ) = SV+ holds.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states this as an open question.

assertions.value: The paper states as open whether every hypergraph quantum automorphism group can be realized as Bichon's quantum automorphism group of a possibly larger classical graph.
quotes: it might be possible that each quantum automorphism group of a hypergraph can be realized as the quantum automorphism group of a possibly larger classical graph.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states this as an open question.

assertions.value: The paper states as open whether a Banica-type version of the quantum automorphism group of hypergraphs exists, one that reduces to Banica's group for classical directed graphs and acts naturally on C*(Γ).
quotes: It also remains open if there exists a Banica version for the quantum automorphism group of hypergraphs
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states this as an open question.

assertions.value: The paper states as open whether Hahn's results on the automorphism group of a product of hypergraphs can be generalized to the quantum setting using the free wreath product of Bichon.
quotes: Can the results of Hahn be generalized to the quantum setting using the free wreath product of Bichon [5]?
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states this as an open question.

papers.title_in_file: A Programmable Spatiotemporal Quantum Parametric Mode Sorter
papers.version_note: arXiv:2210.16517v2, dated 6 Jan 2023; the file name carries 2022 (v1 year).
papers.what_it_is: An experimental paper demonstrating a programmable quantum parametric mode sorter (sum-frequency up-conversion in PPLN) over combined Laguerre-Gaussian spatial and Hermite-Gaussian temporal modes, with pump shaping by an optical arbitrary waveform generator, spatial light modulators and particle swarm optimization.

assertions.value: The authors define a selectivity S, in dB, for each quantum state of the pump, based on the number of sum-frequency photons in the desired mode relative to the other considered modes, as measured with a Si avalanche photodiode.
quotes: we deﬁne the selectivity (S) for each quantum state
as measured using the Si avalanche photo-diode (Si-APD)
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper defines the selectivity metric in Eq. 1 and uses it for all later tables.
assertions.reader_inference: The text layer lost the sum limits of Eq. 1; Table I to IV values are all in this metric, so they are not directly comparable to an extinction ratio defined another way.

assertions.value: The authors state that the information is stored in one of 3 Hermite-Gaussian temporal modes and 5 Laguerre-Gaussian spatial modes, giving 15 spatiotemporal modes, and that each is up-converted by a pump with a unique spatiotemporal profile; they monitor the output for 225 pairs of pump and signal modes.
quotes: To selectively up-convert the signal photons in each of these 15 ST modes, we use a pump with a unique ST mode proﬁle.
We monitor and analyze the SF output for each of the 225 pairs of the ST pump and signal modes.
in a unique quantum state among 3 HG temporal modes |T0 , |T1 , |T2 and 5 LG spatial
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states the size of its mode set in the Model section.
assertions.reader_inference: The spatial modes are restricted to zero radial index, so the 15 modes are a small subset of the full spatiotemporal space.

assertions.value: The authors state that the pump and signal have similar wavelengths under the undepleted pump approximation, so that the inverse group velocity mismatch between them can be neglected and the system operates in the single sideband velocity mismatch (SSVM) regime, in which high mode selectivity is achieved when the pump pulse width is smaller than the temporal walk-off between pump and sum-frequency pulses in the crystal.
quotes: When the temporal pulse width of the
pump is smaller than the temporal walk-oﬀ between the pump and SF pulses in the crystal,
high mode selectivity can be achieved.
assertions.certainty_reason: The condition is stated as a regime result attributed to earlier work ([42, 55]); no derivation is given here.
assertions.reader_inference: The Results section words the same condition as the pump's spectral bandwidth exceeding the phase-matching bandwidth, which is an equivalent statement in the frequency domain.

assertions.value: The authors state that they optimize the pump temporally with particle swarm optimization, adjusting the relative phase of 37 evenly spaced frequency comb lines on an ensemble of 16 candidates, and that the same technique is used to simulate the pump shape for the experiment.
quotes: We further optimize the pump temporally using particle swarm optimization (PSO)
the relative phase of 37 evenly spaced frequency comb lines simultaneously on an ensemble of 16 potential candidates (C).
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own optimization setup in the Model section.
assertions.reader_inference: The Discussion says the optimized pumps in the experiment were prepared numerically ("numerically prepare the optimized pump pulses"), so the optimization is not run in closed loop on the photon counts.

assertions.value: The authors report an experiment in which a 25 GHz optical frequency comb is shaped line by line by a waveshaper to give a pump at 1551 nm and a signal at 1559 nm, each spatially shaped by a spatial light modulator, then combined in a 5 mol.% MgO doped PPLN crystal of length 1 cm or 2.5 cm; the sum-frequency output is coupled into single-mode fiber and detected by a silicon avalanche photodiode.
quotes: The waveshaper provides pump (1551 nm) and signal (1559 nm) separately
We tested two separate nonlinear crystals with lengths 1 cm and 2.5 cm
the SF output is coupled into single-mode ﬁber and detected by a high-speed single-pixel silicon avalanche photodiode (ID100).
generates a phase-coherent broadband frequency comb with a line spacing 25GHz.
(5 mol.% MgO doped PPLN crystal)
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper describes its own apparatus in the Experimental setup section.

assertions.value: The authors report a normalized sum-frequency conversion efficiency of about 1%/W/cm2 and temporal walk-off between pump and sum-frequency pulses of 1.2 ps for the 1 cm crystal and 3 ps for the 2.5 cm crystal.
quotes: normalized conversion eﬃciency of ∼ 1%/W/cm2.
Temporal walk-oﬀ between the pump and SF pulses for 1 cm and 2.5 cm long crystals are 1.2 ps and 3 ps, respectively.
assertions.certainty_reason: A measured device parameter from one setup; the walk-off values come from a sinc-squared fit to the measured phase-matching curve.

assertions.value: The authors report that they measured the phase-matching curve by sweeping the wavelength at constant temperature and fitting an ideal sinc squared curve to it, and obtained temporal walk-off of 1.2 ps and 3 ps for the 1 cm and 2.5 cm crystals; the pump and signal wavelengths are only 8 nm apart.
assertions.anchor: Results, Effect of crystal length on selectivity, p.8
quotes: the wavelengths of our pump and signal are only 8 nm apart.
By ﬁtting this experimental phase matching curve of the nonlinear crystal on top of an ideal sinc2 curve
to be 1.2 ps and 3 ps, respectively.
we evaluated the temporal walk-oﬀ between the pump and SF pulses in the 1 cm and 2.5 cm crystal
assertions.certainty_reason: A measured and fitted device property from one setup.
assertions.reader_inference: The authors tie the 8 nm separation to a limit of the comb generator, so the SSVM regime is a consequence of the setup rather than a design choice.

assertions.value: The authors state that high selectivity in a 1 cm crystal needs a pulse width smaller than 1.2 ps, whose spectral width is over 3 nm and spans near the peak of the phase matching for second harmonic generation, which leads to higher Raman noise; to reduce Raman noise they use pulses over 2 ps with a 1.6 nm spectral bandwidth in the 2.5 cm crystal.

assertions.value: The authors state that optimizing the pumps in the temporal domain only can achieve more than 12 dB extinction for mutually unbiased basis sets of spatiotemporal modes.
quotes: By optimizing pump temporal proﬁles only, we achieve more than 12 dB extinction for mutually unbiased basis (MUB) sets of the spatiotemporal modes.

assertions.value: The authors state, as a technical limitation, that the 25 GHz comb spacing (0.2 nm) gives about 8 comb lines in the 3 dB bandwidth of a 2 ps pulse (spectral FWHM 1.6 nm), which is inadequate to realize temporal modes higher than third order.

we use OFCG with a line spacing of 25 GHz (spectral spacing 0.2 nm)

assertions.value: The authors state that higher-order spatial modes with opposite orbital angular momentum for signal and pump give low photon counts after coupling into the single-mode fiber (about 4 micrometer core diameter), and that few-mode fiber could couple higher-order OAM states but the spatial selectivity would be compromised.
quotes: the higher-order modes in the spatial domain with opposite orbital angular momentum for signal and pump give low photon counts after coupling into the single mode ﬁber (∼4 µm core diameter).
but the spatial selectivity would be compromised.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state the limit of their own setup in the Discussion.
assertions.reader_inference: The abstract credits single-mode fiber coupling with improving mode-sorting performance, while this passage names the same coupling as the cause of low counts for high-order spatial modes.

assertions.value: The authors report that refreshing the waveshaper phase pattern introduces a temporal jitter of about 2 ps between pump and signal, which they handle by scanning the sum-frequency counts over the delay with an optical delay line, and that each pump and signal pair measurement takes about 1 second, which could hinder adaptive optimization of the pump shape using the photon counts as feedback.
quotes: it introduces a temporal jitter of ∼ 2 ps
Our delay and SF count measurement for each pair of pump and signal modes roughly take about 1 second in our Matlab-based interface.
could be a substantial hindrance when it comes to adaptively optimizing the temporal shape of the pump
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state the limit of their own setup in the Discussion.
assertions.reader_inference: The 2 ps jitter equals the pulse width used in most experiments, so a delay scan was needed to find the overlap for every mode pair.

assertions.value: The authors state that spatiotemporal quantum states can form an infinite Hilbert space, increasing the information capacity of a single photon, and that encoding and decoding in these spaces can be beneficial for achieving enhanced key rates for high-dimensional quantum key distribution.
quotes: In principle, ST quantum states can form an inﬁnite Hilbert space, which increases the information capacity of a single photon.
can make it beneﬁcial for achieving enhanced key rates for HD quantum key distribution.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author claim of application benefit; no key rate or protocol is measured in the paper.
assertions.reader_inference: No quantum key distribution protocol, key rate or error rate is demonstrated; the results are classical-light and single-photon-regime selectivities.

assertions.value: The authors propose, without demonstrating it, that heralded and heralding single photons from a spontaneous parametric down-conversion source be selectively up-converted by two identical quantum parametric mode sorters to obtain a single photon source with a highly diminished mode-mismatch, and that individual spatiotemporal modes could be extracted by cascading the scheme in a serial or loop structure.
quotes: by selectively up-converting the output heralded and heralding single photons by using two identical quantum parametric mode sorters
to achieve a single photon source with a highly diminished mode-mismatch.
assertions.certainty_reason: A proposal in the Discussion with no experiment or derivation in the paper.

assertions.value: The authors state that their earlier spatiotemporal mode-selective converter used a spatial light modulator and an optical delay line, and that its delay-only temporal control of Gaussian pulses limited its capacity; this paper adds arbitrary temporal modulation by an optical arbitrary waveform generator.
quotes: It has a limited capacity due to the delay-only temporal control of the Gaussian pulses
we overcome the aforementioned restriction of our previous study by adding arbitrary temporal modulation
assertions.certainty_reason: A statement about earlier work (ref. 47) by the same group.

assertions.value: The authors state that nonlinear-optical mode sorting techniques have an upper hand over linear counterparts because they can manipulate single photons without any loss.
quotes: as they can manipulate single photons without any loss.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author claim about a technique class, stated without evidence in this paper.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper reports a normalized conversion efficiency of about 1%/W/cm2 and a waveshaper insertion loss of about 4.5 dB, but no end-to-end single-photon efficiency, so the lossless statement is an ideal-case claim, not a measured one.

assertions.value: The authors state that extension to noisy conditions, namely spatial turbulence and time-frequency noise overlapping the signal modes, is future work, so the reported results do not include such noise.
quotes: In the future, we can extend our HD quantum mode-sorting approach for more practical scenarios, such as passing through a noisy environment due to spatial turbulence [37] and/or time-frequency noises [41]
assertions.certainty_reason: The Conclusion states the scope of the work and defers noisy conditions.
